title: The northern roads, closed
hookLine: China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, Mongolia, the West

lines: A TONGUE, A SKULL, A SHIP.
cards: A tongue that would not burn. Water drunk from a skull in the dark. A bronze Buddha on a ship.
Two niches in a cliff, holding nothing. A palace on a hill. A cup of tea running over the rim.

A few of the things this path has picked up on one long road: from the tree in northern India north over the mountains, east to the sea, up onto the plateau, out to the grasslands, and across an ocean to Chicago.

teach.b: Monks and merchants carried the teaching along the caravan roads of the Silk Road. Kumarajiva translated sutras into Chinese, and the story says his tongue did not burn.
Faxian walked to India, and Xuanzang crossed the desert, tradition says against the emperor's ban, and came home with the texts.

Bodhidharma, the story goes, told an emperor his temples earned no merit, and a woodcutter named Huineng, who couldn't write, asked someone to put his verse on a wall. Guanyin heard the cries of the world.
In Korea, Wonhyo drank water from a skull in the dark and woke up to his own mind. The whole canon was carved into woodblocks, and carved again after a fire.
A bronze Buddha crossed the sea from Korea to Japan; the great Buddha rose at Nara; monks climbed Mount Hiei and Koyasan, and new schools grew.
In Tibet, a king invited an abbot; Padmasambhava came; Samye was built; a debate was held. After the quiet years, a translator walked to India, Atisha came, and the canons were gathered.
A line of Dalai Lamas, a palace on a hill, a Mongol ruler who gave the title ocean of wisdom. Empty niches at Bamiyan, a sealed cave at Dunhuang, and in Vietnam, a king who became a monk.

Then across the oceans: translators carried the texts into English, a poem told the Buddha's life, two Buddhists spoke in Chicago, Zen came west, temples endured, Tibetans taught in exile, insight traveled, and now the sangha is everywhere, even on a screen.
Tomorrow a new part of the path begins: the great teachers.

how: Buddhists in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Tibet, Mongolia and the West each keep the forms the teaching took on its way to them, and pilgrims still travel these roads to the temples and sites along them.

o: the caravan roads that carried the teaching to China
a single highway running from India to Rome
the road pilgrims walk around a holy mountain

games.q: the northern roads: tap the pairs.
p: crossed the desert for the texts
drank water from a skull in the dark
came to Tibet after the dark years
two Buddhists spoke for the teaching

s: the teaching reached Japan by way of Korea
a bronze Buddha crossed the sea from Korea.
the northern roads ended in Tibet
they ran on to Mongolia, and then across the oceans to the West.
Huineng wrote his verse on the wall in his own hand
he couldn't write; he asked someone to put it on the wall for him.

games.q: you're Xuanzang at the edge of the desert. the emperor has forbidden travel west, and the texts you need are in India. what do you do?
o: send a letter asking for the texts.
games.why: tradition says Xuanzang went without permission, crossed the desert, studied in India and came home with the texts.

practice: With a finger in the air, or only in your mind, trace the road: northern India, over the mountains, east along the Silk Road to China, Korea, then Japan, back to Tibet, out to Mongolia, then across the ocean to the West.
At each stop, pause for one breath and let one picture come: a desert, a skull cup, a bronze Buddha, a palace, a hall in Chicago. Then rest, and sit.

wordCard.voice: Silk Road. The caravan roads that carried monks, merchants and the teaching north and east from India, through Kumarajiva, Faxian and Xuanzang, into China.

carryVoice: Your line: it traveled far. From one tree to many shores. That's the northern roads, done.
